intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that brain small vessel disease-4 (BSVD4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NIT1 gene (604618) on chromosome 1q23.3.

checks.claim: Brain small vessel disease-4 (BSVD4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NIT1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The first identified patients were 3 siblings, compound heterozygous for the NIT1 c.727C>T; (p.Arg243Trp) variant and the NIT1 c.198_199del; p.(Ala68∗) variant. The 4 additional patients were single cases from 4 unrelated pedigrees and were all homozygous
checks.explanation: The paper reports homozygous and compound heterozygous NIT1 variants causing the disease. BSVD4 is the OMIM name for it.

checks.evidence_quote: two rare variants were found in the NIT1 gene (Nitrilase‐like protein 1, NM_005600)
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature restating the gene identified in the paper.

paragraphs.text: Brain small vessel disease-4 is an autosomal recessive disorder. It presents in adulthood with neurologic and psychiatric signs, and brain imaging shows cystic, cavitating lesions or massively dilated perivascular spaces in the basal ganglia. Rendu et al. (2019) described it as a metabolic disorder that combines neurologic signs, cavitating lesions of the basal ganglia, and a positive urine sulfite test. Rutten et al. (2024) described NIT1-small vessel disease as a cerebral small vessel disease characterized by a triad of movement disorders, massively dilated basal ganglia perivascular spaces, and intracerebral hemorrhage.

checks.evidence_quote: Adult genetic disorders causing brain lesions have been mostly described as white matter vanishing diseases. We present here the investigations realized in patients referred for psychiatric disorder

paragraphs.text: Rendu et al. (2019) reported 3 affected brothers from 1 family with a familial deep cavitating state. The index patient (II.4) was admitted to an emergency ward at age 34 years for a sudden left hemiparesis. He had a history of nonsevere mental retardation. Two years earlier he had been admitted to a psychiatry unit for an acute psychotic episode followed by generalized seizures. Imaging showed bilateral small cystic lesions of the basal ganglia. Arteriography, EEG, EMG, Doppler ultrasound, and cardiac echocardiography were normal. A dipstick urine test for sulfites was positive. Over a 20-year period his condition progressively worsened, with severe neuropsychological deterioration and spastic tetraplegia. He died in 2011, and no autopsy was performed.

paragraphs.text: In 2014, a brother (II.5) of the index patient in the family reported by Rendu et al. (2019) was admitted to intensive care at age 58 years for a sudden coma with cardiovascular collapse. He had a history of diabetes mellitus and had lived an active professional life. He had basal ganglia cystic lesions, and his urine sulfite test was also positive. He gradually recovered but had neuropsychological deterioration (BREF, 14/18; MMSE, 22/30). A third brother (II.7), age 60 years, had been in a psychiatric institution for schizophrenia diagnosed 40 years earlier. His clinical examination was normal, but CT and 3-T MRI showed the same brain lesions, and his urine sulfite test was positive.

paragraphs.text: Rutten et al. (2024) reported 7 patients with NIT1-related small vessel disease: 3 sibs and 4 single cases from 4 unrelated pedigrees. The patients presented in mid-adulthood with movement disorders. All had striking abnormalities on brain MRI, with numerous and massively dilated basal ganglia perivascular spaces. Three of the 7 patients had a nonlobar intracerebral hemorrhage between ages 45 and 60 years, which was fatal in 2. Brain autopsy showed large electron-dense deposits in the vessel walls of small and medium-sized cerebral arteries.

paragraphs.text: Using GC/MS, Rendu et al. (2019) found a deaminated glutathione (dGSH) derivative in the urine of the 3 affected brothers. It was absent from the urine of their unaffected sibs and their mother. Its mass spectrum resembled that of the compound seen in Nit1-knockout mice, and the authors suggested that dGSH probably caused the positive urine sulfite test. In patient fibroblasts, mitochondrial MnSOD activity was increased twofold, while cytoplasmic Cu/Zn SOD activity was unchanged.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of BSVD4 is autosomal recessive. In the family reported by Rendu et al. (2019), 3 brothers were affected, and the affected brothers who were genotyped were compound heterozygous for NIT1 mutations. One mutation was inherited from their asymptomatic mother, and asymptomatic sibs carried neither mutation. Rutten et al. (2024) found homozygous or compound heterozygous NIT1 mutations in affected sibs and in single cases from unrelated pedigrees.

paragraphs.text: Rendu et al. (2019) suspected an inherited recessive disorder in 3 affected brothers with a deep cavitating state and performed exome sequencing on 2 of them (II.5 and II.7). Both were compound heterozygous for 2 rare NIT1 mutations: a c.457G-A transition (gly153-to-arg, G153R) and a 1-bp duplication (c.670dupA), predicted to cause a frameshift and premature termination (Thr224AsnfsTer41). The c.670dupA mutation was inherited from the asymptomatic mother, and the asymptomatic sibs carried neither mutation. Molecular cloning showed that the 2 mutations were on different alleles. The c.457G-A mutation affects the last nucleotide of exon 4 and disrupted splicing in transcripts from patient skin. NIT1 protein could not be detected by Western blot in patient fibroblasts.

paragraphs.text: Rutten et al. (2024) studied 7 patients with brain small vessel disease. Three sibs were compound heterozygous for 2 NIT1 mutations: a c.727C-T transition (arg243-to-trp, R243W) and a 2-bp deletion (c.198_199del) causing a premature stop (Ala68Ter). The other 4 patients were single cases from 4 unrelated pedigrees, and all were homozygous for the R243W mutation. Western blotting of patient fibroblasts showed no NIT1 protein, and metabolic analysis of urine confirmed loss of NIT1 enzymatic function, consistent with loss-of-function mutations.
